title: Session 2 – Descriptive Statistics & Visual Data Analysis

children: Nominal: no hierarchy (gender, product categories, regions)
Ordinal: hierarchy (age groups, purchase frequency)
Interval: equal intervals, no true zero (Likert scales, NPS, brand attitude)
Ratio: equal intervals and a true zero (age, income, revenues, sales)

blocks.text: A questionnaire is a series of structured, mostly closed-ended questions. Use clear, brief language, a natural flow, never lead the respondent, and open with the research purpose, anonymity/privacy and instructions. Content can cover facts, awareness, behaviour frequency, opinions, motivations, intentions, attitudes, demographics and psychographics.
Question types determine the variable type:
children: Dichotomous (yes/no): nominal
Rank order: ordinal
Multiple choice – select one: nominal or ordinal; select many: nominal (add "don't know" / "other")
Likert scale (5, 7 or 9 points; semantic differential or matrix): metric interval
CSAT = satisfied customers (4 and 5) / responses × 100
NPS = % promoters (9–10) − % detractors (0–6) – measures loyalty
CES = customers agreeing (5, 6, 7) that the company made it easy / responses × 100
Frequencies: absolute and relative (share of the sample)
Central tendency: mean (metric), median (not for nominal), mode (any variable)
Dispersion: variance (average squared deviation from the mean) and standard deviation (its square root, same unit) – metric only

blocks.text: Bivariate/multivariate analysis examines two or more variables. The Pearson correlation coefficient (−1 to 1) shows direction and strength of a linear relationship between metric variables – not causation.

Visual data analysis helps people make sense of and interact with massive data sets; data visualisation converts raw data into easily understood pictures that enable fast and effective decisions (visual analytics process model, Keim et al., 2010).

children: Five hat racks (LATCH): location, alphabet, time, category, hierarchy
Visual variables: size, orientation, shape, colour, value, texture
Check data source, statistics, aesthetics, coordinates (no cut scales), position, guides, geometry, colour-blind-friendly themes, manipulation
Bar: compare categories or change over time, positive and negative values, ≤ 10 bars
Pie: proportions, ≤ 6–7 categories
Line: continuous data over time, several series, trends
Area: part-to-whole and volume
Scatter: correlation and clustering; histogram: distribution
Gauge/bullet: performance against a target (KPIs, NPS); radar: compare several features

blocks.text: In Stata you work with the result window, command window, history and variables list, and save your commands in a do-file (Superstore dataset exercise).
Analysis of a single variable (frequencies, central tendency, dispersion).
Examines two (bivariate) or more variables; usually one dependent and several independent variables.
The most frequent score of a variable – the highest bar in a histogram; computable for any variable.
The middle score of data arranged by magnitude; not computable for nominal variables.
Square root of the variance; measures how spread out observations are, in the unit of the mean.
Procedures to present, navigate, aggregate and see details of data so that complex questions can be answered.
